title: Meteors that skim the sky, the sunset's green patch explained and gone, clearer water, and gold that reads as gold
intro: Your round 9 answers are built in: the fast volumetrics stay on, daytime torchlight stays damped, the sun stays behind its cloud, and the noon clouds keep the cheaper version. What changed: Meteors are rebuilt as Earth-grazers, the 'passing by at high altitude' you asked for. The shower's radiant sits on the horizon, so every meteor skims the upper air about 100 km up on a long, near-level path for 2 to 5 seconds and leaves a thin tapering trail; each is drawn as a real 3D track, so the ones overhead sweep across the sky and the far ones creep along the horizon. The green patch in the middle of the sunset was the sky seen through the sea: where no sea bed is in view, the water showed the sky behind it, and at sunset that is the brightest thing in the frame; the water then took out the red and left mint. Deep water with no bed in view now shows only its own colour. Under water the fog is thinned 2x: the far canyon wall shows 41% more contrast, with the same blue look you liked. The river is teal-blue instead of green. Gold was darker than vanilla under the shader (1.48x the stone beside it against vanilla's 1.82x) because the colour grade clipped its blue channel to zero in 61% of its pixels and the metal kept too little of its diffuse light; now 1.74x, nothing clipped, and gold reflects with real gold's colour, so its lime sheen is gone. Not changed, honestly: the forest's rays (three tries made no visible difference; see that scene), the dust in the beam and the golden plains. Cost: High frames cost 3.5 ms at most (round 9: 3.3, budget 3.0), Low at 1080p 0.89 ms (budget 0.9), Potato at 720p 0.31 ms (budget 0.4). Costs are per frame against the same view with shaders off. Over the High budget: the night skies with the new meteors (3.42 and 3.47 ms; round 9 2.99), and the same sunset and water views as round 9 (3.04 to 3.31 ms, within 0.03 ms of round 9). Two cost questions: how many meteors (the meteors scene) and crepuscular rays round the setting sun (the sun-cloud scene). After the shader questions come the textures (the wall explained, three leaf directions, the farm), the leaf frills and the crop variants. Credits: Faithful 32x and 64x (faithfulpack.net, Faithful License v4) in the QF Textures and Faithful frames; the normal and specular maps are converted from Vanilla Normals Renewed by Poudingue (github.com/Poudingue/Vanilla-Normals-Renewed-1.12).

scenes.name: Meteors: grazers at high altitude (motion clips)
scenes.question: You said round 9's meteors were 'plummeting to the ground' and asked for a cinematic shower 'passing by at high altitude'. Cause: round 9 put the radiant (the point a shower streams from) high in the sky, so the streaks pointed down at the horizon. Real showers seen when the radiant has just risen are Earth-grazers: the meteors enter almost level, skim the air about 100 km up, burn for seconds instead of a fraction of one, and cross a large part of the sky. That is now the default. Two directions, same view, clips at game speed: A grazers (about one in flight at a time, 24 meteor slots); B a grazer storm (40 slots, three times the rate, mostly faint, longer trails). C is round 9's shower. A third direction, a rare slow fireball breaking into a chain of fragments, was tried and dropped: in its test clip it dived steeply from the top of the frame with two or three fragments and vanished in one frame, the plummeting look you rejected, not a procession. Cost: each meteor slot is tested per sky pixel, so the grazers cost more than round 9's flat streaks: the night-sky frame 2.88 ms on High (round 9: 2.46 ms); this wide view A 3.43 ms and B 3.98 ms, both over the 3.0 ms High budget (night skies are the only frames that are). Trade-off: B fills the sky but makes each meteor less of an event and costs 0.55 ms more than A (about 0.03 ms per slot); halving A to 12 slots would save about 0.41 ms, which still leaves the wide view a little over budget, with half as many meteors in the sky.
scenes.notePrompt: Is this the shower you pictured? A or B as the default? Fewer meteors to get back under budget?

options.label: Grazers (new default), clip
options.critic: Critic 8: The ask is met: long, thin, near-level streaks skimming parallel to the horizon with tapering trails, never diving at the ground; one or two in flight at a time reads as a calm shower. Against the photo reference the sky itself is still flat (no Milky Way band, few bright stars), and heavy night clouds hide half the sky. Fix: fewer slots or a cheaper per-slot test (3.47 ms, over the 3.0 budget).

options.label: Grazer storm, clip
options.critic: Critic 7: Storm: six to eight parallel streaks at once, all from one direction, which sells the shower better than A in a still, but each one is fainter and the sky starts to look busy; it costs 0.55 ms more than A (3.98 ms on High). A as the default with an occasional storm night would be the better mix.

scenes.name: The sunset's green patch: cause and fix
scenes.question: You saw 'some weird green coloring right in the middle of the image'. Cause, found with a debug view that shows only what lies behind the water: in that wedge the sea bed is out of view, so the water showed the sky behind it in the screen, and at sunset that is the bright glow round the sun. The water absorbed its red over 32 blocks and left green and blue, a mint wedge (151,185,130). Real deep water has no sky behind it; with no bed in view it now shows only its own in-scattered colour, and the sun's path and the reflected sky are untouched. (Two earlier tries this round, a fix to the reflections and dimming the sunlight on shallow sand, cut it from 1107 px to 686 px; this removes the cause: 0 px of mint left in the same box.) Cost: none (one comparison). A is new, B round 9; C and D the same wedge cropped at twice the size.

scenes.name: The sun and its clouds: crepuscular rays (cost question)
scenes.question: You asked that the sun interact realistically with the clouds in front of it. Two changes. Built in: clouds near a low sun no longer melt into the haze (they faded to about 20% at that distance while still hiding the disk, so a hidden sun sat behind a cloud you could barely see); now the cloud in front is a solid body with lit edges. A brighter silver lining on the thinnest edges made no visible difference (0.5 luma in this crop), so it was dropped. Your call: crepuscular rays, the lit lanes and shadow wedges that fan out from a sun behind broken cloud. They read the clouds' shadow along the line to the sun: 16 extra texture reads per sky pixel near a low sun, on High and Ultra only. Measured on High at 1440p: 0.33 ms extra at most (ocean_sunset 3.31 ms without, 3.64 ms with; budget 3.0); at noon they switch off (sky_noon +0.04 ms). In this view they draw a fan of lit lanes and shadow wedges in the clear gap above the sun (the wedges about 7% darker); the whole sunset (D) shows it best. Trade-off: the sunset frame is already 0.3 ms over budget without them. A new without rays, B with rays, both cropped round the sun at twice the size; C round 9; D the whole sunset with rays.

scenes.name: Forest light: longer, broader rays
scenes.question: You liked that round 9's B had rays that 'extend further and seem a bit broader'. B's rays were longer because the beam haze was not cut on rays that end on leaves; that cut is what removed the cream veil from the canopy. B here keeps the full haze on rays longer than about 20 m (so far beams reach the far leaves) and doubles the shaft strength. Honest result: in this view it measures within 1 luma of A, so it is not the leap you asked for; the rays here are limited by how few gaps the canopy has toward the sun, not by the haze. Cost: B 2.05 ms against A's 2.03 ms. A new (default), B longer rays, C round 9.

scenes.name: Gold and iron under the shader
scenes.question: You asked why gold and iron looked wrong; the texture side is in the wall scene below, the rest was the shader. Measured against the plain stone beside it: vanilla gold 1.82x, round 9's shader 1.48x. Two causes: the vibrance step pushed gold's weakest colour (blue) below zero, clipped in 61% of its pixels, and a metal kept only 30% of its diffuse light under the reflection. Now vibrance never takes a colour below half its value, metals keep 62%, and gold reflects with real gold's colour instead of the texture's, which the grade had turned lime. Gold now 1.74x, nothing clipped. Cost: none (2.22 ms against round 9's settings at 2.22 ms). A new, B round 9's metal settings, C shaders off (vanilla light), D the whole wall, new.

scenes.name: The block wall: why diamond was lit only at the bottom
scenes.question: Cause, in one sentence: the normal maps we convert from Vanilla Normals Renewed were already in the shader's convention and our converter flipped them again, so 34 blocks were lit from below, and on diamond, which VNR also flags as metal (a mirror), the flipped dome mirrored the dark ground on its top half and the sky on its bottom half. Measured on one diamond face (mean brightness, top half / bottom half): round 9 127 / 167; normals fixed only 176 / 122 (the split just reverses, because a mirror still shows ground and sky); normals fixed and diamond a gem 165 / 136, the same average as Faithful (150). Iron now matches vanilla (1.82x the stone beside it). Gold is still darker than vanilla (1.52x stone vs 1.71x) under every texture option, Faithful's too: the shader's colour grade clips gold's blue to zero, now fixed on the shader side (the gold scene above; these frames were shot before that fix). Look at gold's top third in B: a lime sheen. That is the metal mirroring the green field, tinted by gold's colour; the shader fix is to use real gold reflectance instead of the texture colour, now in: see the gold scene above.

scenes.name: Leaves up close: three directions
scenes.question: Restarted from licensed art as you asked: no code-drawn leaves. Three different directions, all from Faithful's own leaves. A is Faithful 64x as is (your round 9 pick). B fills each block's holes with darker copies of the same leaves so a canopy reads as a mass, keeping the ragged outline. C goes for Stay True's grain: Faithful 32x's smaller leaves, four times as many per block, lit crowns, dark undersides. Trade-off: A shows the most sky and the most shape per block but reads thin; C reads densest and most like the reference but each leaf is smaller, so up close it is busier. A first try at a fully opaque version turned every block into a hard green cube and was dropped. Honest limit: B's and C's ragged rim only shows up close; from a few blocks away a canopy's outline is still stepped cubes. A texture cannot fix that; the leaf frills (a separate question this round) are the fix, and they take whichever leaf you pick.

scenes.name: The farm: Stay True's technique on Faithful's wheat
scenes.question: Stay True's field reads as one gold mass because each ripe block is a dense bush of gold, dark at the base and pale at the tips, and five versions of different heights are mixed so the field never tiles. A and B rebuild that from Faithful 64x's own plant: layered four deep, recoloured to a six-step gold ramp; A also stacks extra ear heads across the top. Honest limit: the five heights do not show yet. Our 1.7.10 renderer never applies random textures to crops (it does to grass and blocks), so every block draws the same middle height here. The small hook you approved now does it (the crop-variant scenes at the end); carrots (4) and potatoes (4, two with white flowers) get variants too.

scenes.name: Leaf frills: the hedge
scenes.question: You picked real outward leaf frills like Stay True's. Why our hedges look like boxes: a leaf block is a cube, so its outline is twelve straight edges. The frills add leaf cards (the texture agent's frill sprite: whole Faithful leaves, solid at the base) leaning out of every edge that has air on both sides, so the outline turns ragged. Four looks were tried; cards out of the face centres and hanging cards read as streaks and smears and were dropped. B and C are the two best. Trade-off: more vertices in leafy chunks (B +42%, C +29%) and slower chunk rebuilds there (B +11%, C +9%); frame time did not move beyond noise on this PC. It has its own switch, so Low and Potato keep it off.
